body.text: Canva announces an overhaul affecting 22 per cent of its workforce, with jobs to be lost in a restructure affecting more than 1,200 people.
Futures point to a modestly lower open for the Australian share market as the US midterms come into sharp focus.
Investors on Wall Street have moved back into big tech stocks, but the NASDAQ remains in correction territory.

'Deal with it': RBA and its inflation fight

It's an upside down world. People complain about inflation hurting them, then they complain when the RBA (belatedly?) takes action to combat inflation. The reality of our system is rates go up enough to slow spending, shutter businesses and raise unemployment which will reduce inflation (if the government doesn't splash more cash). Obviously raising rates causes pain. Deal with it, it will happen again in your lifetime.
Thanks for the blog contribution Topsy Turvy.
Goodman says 'demand for digital infrastructure continues'
Industrial real estate manager Goodman Group says its data centre development projects are “on track”.
It's posted a first quarter 2027 operational update to the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).

Goodman says it expects, “growing demand and constrained supply to continue to support rental growth, creating further opportunities to develop our assets, and grow the value of our business around the world”.
Canva redundancies global
Canva CEO Melanie Perkins's update on the firm's restructure today alludes to a global round of redundancies:
"Our immediate priority is to make time for the conversations with everyone directly impacted by these changes.
"Those impacted will receive a calendar invite for an individual meeting with a senior leader in their area to discuss the next steps and support available should they wish to attend.

"With teams across 37 countries, we'll need to follow different local requirements and processes, which means the timing and way these conversations happen may vary depending on where people are based."

'Robust momentum' for US economy
Here's MooMoo's Michael McCarthy's take on the economic data drops out of the US overnight.
"The macroeconomic landscape continues to demonstrate robust momentum alongside stubborn yield pressures.
"US job vacancies topped expectations at 7.5 million, while the 'voluntary quits' rate rose to 2.1%. This suggests the low-hire, low-fire labour market is starting to heat back up.
"Consequently, the US 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.96%.
"Meta's recent debt issuance is a timely reminder of the deluge of debt funding the AI boom, with its yield premium to treasuries widening significantly to 190 basis points from 90 in April."
Westpac sees RBA pausing on rates in December
The RBA lifted the cash rate yesterday to 4.85% on domestic inflation, oil price pass-through and the AI boom.
Westpac's chief economist Luci Ellis says the "split vote and shifting risks make a December pause likely".
Watchdog fines companies for lack of disclosure
ASIC has issued infringement notices to 22 large proprietary companies for allegedly failing to lodge their audited financial reports on time for the 2025 financial year.
The notices were issued as part of ASIC's ongoing surveillance and enforcement work focused on financial reporting compliance.
The 22 companies have paid their infringement notices in full. Each infringement notice is $198,000, totalling $4,356,000 across the 22 companies.

Oil price and renewed hopes for Middle East diplomacy
Barclays has penned a note on movements in the oil market.

• Oil prices have weakened on renewed US-Iran diplomatic optimism, but there is still little evidence of a substantive breakthrough at this time. On the surface, there is little change in the Iranian position, but it is difficult to tell how much of that is just posturing.

• Regardless, signs of somewhat greater flexibility in Iran should be weighed against the evolving political risk-reward in the US, especially given relatively subdued speculative positioning and options skew, strong physical markers and a potentially fatter right tail that a continuation of the recent status quo would warrant, in our view.
• We maintain our Brent forecasts of $100/b in 2026 and $85/b in 2027, and recommend a tactical long in September minus December 2027 Brent calendar spread, at $3.40/b at the time of writing.

Canva not replacing roles with AI
Software company Canva has announced a major corporate restructuring that will affect 1,271 roles.
There is no reference to artificial intelligence (AI) as a reason for the redundancies.
The ABC understands the changes are about setting Canva up to build AI-related products, not using AI to do the work of people who are leaving.
Key Event
Canva 'exploring a wide range of alternatives'
Software company Canva has announced it's embarking on a major organisational restructure.
Here are the reasons CEO Melanie Perkins gave for the decision to axe more than 1,000 roles.

"To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community."This means:

This means
• "Simplifying how we come together to build Canva.
• "We're reducing subspecialisation and collapsing layers to broaden ownership.
• "We're co-locating closely connected teams and increasing in-person collaboration."

Perkins said: "Sydney will become the primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important."We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we're committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support."

'Profoundly difficult news to share': Canva axes more than 1,000 staff
Software company Canva has just announced a big round of redundancies.
Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins just sent the following note to staff:

"After months of thinking through how to set Canva up for the next chapter, we have made the incredibly hard decision to make significant changes to how we're organised, where some of our teams are based, and the roles and skills we need for the future.

"This means 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva, will be impacted. For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.

"This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history. Behind every decision is someone we care deeply about, and I know the consequences will be very real for those directly affected, their families, friends and teammates.

"I'm deeply sorry for the pain and disruption this will cause for everyone affected. While nothing can make this news easier, we will do everything we possibly can to support everyone affected. I want to explain as openly as I can why we're making these changes, how we reached these decisions, and, most importantly, how we will care for the people affected today."

Data centres and inflation pressure
Advisory firm Deloitte Access Economics has been looking at the impact of enormous amounts of data centre spending on inflation.
Here's an excerpt from its report just published.

Australia's data centre boom is landing on top of an already record construction pipeline, with the value of projects under construction approaching $870 billion in 2027 — more than double the peak of the mining boom. It comes at a time when the economy has little spare capacity to absorb it and inflation remains above target.

"Australia's investment pipeline has reached a record $1.39 trillion, including 37 data centre projects worth $141 billion, up 36% over the past year," Deloitte Access Economics director and lead author Sheraan Underwood said.
"Data centres are the newest driver, but they're being added to a pipeline that is already historically large.
"Transport and social infrastructure investment is still elevated, and it now overlaps with the net zero transition and the build-out of the digital economy.
"The current cycle differs from the mining boom in three ways: where the activity is happening, the economy's capacity to absorb it, and the eventual payoff.

"New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland account for 67% of data centre investment in the database. During the mining boom, around 80% of investment went to Western Australia, South Australia and the Northern Territory.
"This boom is happening close to our major cities, so data centres are competing directly with housing and infrastructure for workers and materials.

"There's also less room to absorb it than during the mining boom. Inflation is above the Reserve Bank's target and the construction sector is already dealing with a historically large volume of work," Underwood said.

It's time to go back to the 'sales tax' system instead of GST. Having variable rates for different items and giving the RBA the power to 'target' different rates for discretionary expenditure would result in immediate demand reduction for high-end and non-essential goods. It worked fine.- Phillip

Oil swings on 'mixed headlines'
The National Australia Bank has published a morning note on oil market movements overnight.
Here's the guts of it
Oil swung as markets were back to headline volatility.
Brent traded up towards $107 before falling below $101 and then retracing to sit around $103.7, down 1% over the day.
Optimism on signs of diplomacy drove the selloff, but that was pared after Iran said the US response to its demands wasn't "satisfactory" and that no new developments had been reached.
US President Donald Trump also said that the US would cut off military aid to Israel by the end of the year, suggesting the phase-out of grants could occur much faster than expected.
Key Event
Australian dollar eases further overnight
The Australian dollar eased further to near 69.7 US cents.
The AUD/USD has been weighed down by the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) split decision to raise the cash rate by 25bp yesterday.
Here's an excerpt from the CBA's morning foreign exchange note "Asia Open".
Yesterday's rate hike was the fifth hike of 2026 and took the cash rate to the highest level since 2008.
Our Australian economics team expects this to be the last hike of the cycle but notes the risks remain skewed to further tightening next year.
Meanwhile, we expect two, and possibly three, Federal Reserve rate hikes by March 2027.
The implication is Australia's interest rate advantage over the US will narrow, diminishing the tailwind for AUD/USD in coming months.
'Like they don't care': Mortgage pain hits hard
Yesterday's Reserve Bank interest rate hike, the fifth this year, will put more pressure on households.
Those with large loan repayments, the unemployed and renters could struggle to stretch their budgets.
Nassim Khadem and I spoke to Australians who said they were struggling with seemingly endless expenses.
Key Event
'Less than a week's cover for essentials': survey
AMP has just published the results of a household budget survey.
The investment firms says it shows "just how thin the financial buffer is for many Australian households, particularly following the RBA's rate rise".
Key findings include
• Everyday bills and expenses are cited as the biggest financial concern for 32%.
• One in six (17%) say they could cover essential expenses for less than a week if their income suddenly stopped.
• More than a third (37%) say they have less than a month's cover.
• 36% say they're financially worse off than 12 months ago.
• 27% describe themselves as financially "treading water", while 12% say they're "falling behind".
• One in three (33%) single parents say they have less than a week's cover.
"Another rate rise means households already stretched may need to find more money in budgets with very little give," AMP Bank Group executive Sean O'Malley said.
"Some will cut discretionary spending further, draw on savings or mortgage prepayments, while those under greater pressure may need to speak to their bank about repayment arrangements.
"The important thing is not to wait until you're in serious financial difficulty before looking at your options."
Key Event
Investors move back into tech as fears ease
The Nasdaq rallied overnight as AI heavyweights rebounded ahead of US midterm election results.
Apple fell after the iPhone maker joined the list of Big Tech companies whose quarterly results failed to impress investors.
Wall Street's fear index, the VIX, fell 2% overnight as investors shed some nerves about both the AI trade and the oil price.

But investors are getting nervous about market resiliency. US President Donald Trump's erratic trade policies and the Iran war's energy shock have revived inflation worldwide, putting pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. That, along with AI's capital-investment surge and highly indebted governments, is driving up borrowing costs to multidecade highs.

With US midterms volatile geopolitics and central bank policy promising further uncertainty in the final stretch of the year, some investors and economists say risks to the global economy are mounting.
"Rising rates always seem to sniff out and expose the most vulnerable time after time," former Goldman Sachs chief economist Jim O'Neill said."Countries and businesses too exposed suffer the most."

Welcome to the ABC business blog
Good morning and welcome to the ABC's business blog.
Wall Street's fear index, the VIX, shed 2 per cent overnight as some confidence re-emerged in the market.
A falling oil price seems to be helping on that front.
In terms of stocks, there looks to have been some rotation out of industrial stocks and into the big tech names.
Apple was the exception there, falling almost 2% after disappointing iPad sales results in the fiscal fourth-quarter missed the Street’s estimates.
Let's get going and look to US equities, the midterms, oil price and the ASX open of trade.
